name: Chair work (Alexander)

card.summary: A guided sit-to-stand and sit-down practice from the Alexander Technique that people use to retrain posture, giving a more upright, balanced carriage.
card.note: Taught as an educational method; health-condition claims are reviewed differently by different bodies.

quick.overview:
Chair work is the core exercise of the Alexander Technique: a teacher guides a student through sitting down and standing up while attending to head, neck and back coordination. People interested in appearance use it because slouching, forward head posture and collapsed shoulders change how tall and open someone looks.

The method was developed by actor F.M. Alexander (1869-1955) after he worked on a recurring voice problem. Published reviews have mostly examined the technique as a whole, with findings on back pain and some other conditions; none has measured how chair work alters perceived appearance.
quick.how: Lessons are usually private, last 30 to 60 minutes, and combine spoken cues with light hands-on guidance, often in front of a mirror. Students practise sitting, standing and walking, then carry the habit into daily activities such as desk work.
quick.risks: The technique is gentle and taught as education rather than treatment. The UK is not statutorily regulating it, so teachers belong to voluntary bodies. The NHS and several insurers describe the evidence for many claimed benefits as limited.

lead: Chair work is the signature exercise of the Alexander Technique, in which a student is guided through sitting down and standing up while attending to how the head, neck and back coordinate [1]. It is usually done with a teacher, often in front of a mirror, and the same approach is applied to walking and standing [1].

For appearance, the interest is posture. Habitual slumping, a jutting head and rounded shoulders shorten the visible frame and close the chest; people who practise chair work do so to stand and sit with a longer, more balanced line. The Technique originated with F.M. Alexander (1869-1955), an actor who developed its principles from the 1890s to overcome recurrent laryngitis [1].
Reviews of the Technique have looked at back pain, Parkinson's disease, performance anxiety and other topics, not at appearance outcomes [1].

chain: Guided sit-to-stand with attention to head-neck-back coordination
Less habitual slumping and neck strain
angle.text: Chair work retrains how a person sits and rises, which students apply to daily posture. People use it to hold the head and trunk in a taller, more open line when seated and standing.

infobox: Not statutorily regulated; voluntary professional bodies [1]

paras: In the Alexander Technique, chair work guides a student through standing, sitting and walking, commonly with a mirror, using verbal direction and gentle touch [1]. Table work, in which the teacher manipulates a lying student, is the other main format [1]. The aim described by practitioners is to help people notice and avoid habits that add tension, rather than to cure an underlying cause [1].

Alexander was an actor whose career was hampered by voice loss. He found that attending to his own tension and releasing it helped, and he began formulating the method in the 1890s; a recital tour of New Zealand in 1895 led him to link posture with general functioning [1]. The philosopher John Dewey was impressed by the results he experienced and wrote the introduction to Alexander's 1923 book; Fritz Perls credited Alexander as an inspiration for Gestalt therapy [1].

Posture affects how tall and how broad a person looks, so those working on their physical presentation sometimes take Alexander lessons or practise the sit-stand sequence at home. The mirror component of chair work gives visual feedback on head and shoulder position. The practice is discussed in height and posture circles as a free alternative to gear, though no study has measured its visual effect.

A 2014 review characterised the Technique as an educational approach rather than a medical treatment [1]. A 2015 Australian Department of Health review found it may improve short-term pain and disability in low back pain, with longer-term effects uncertain [1]. The NHS and NICE report that evidence suggests possible help for chronic back and neck pain and for people with Parkinson's, and NICE suggests considering it alongside physiotherapy for Parkinson's with balance problems [1]. A 2012 Cochrane review found no good evidence for asthma, and one insurer classes the method as experimental [1].
No studies found on chair work's effect on appearance. Studies of the Alexander Technique as a whole are summarised above; trials are generally small [1].
